evals.name: seed-offer-ai-app
evals.prompt: We're 2 founders building an AI tool that handles insurance claim paperwork for dental clinics. We're at $18k MRR, growing about 12% a month, and we have about 9 months of runway from our own savings. A seed fund has offered $3M at a $15M post-money valuation. Should we take it? And honestly how much should we even be raising right now?
evals.expected_output: Uses fundraising and survival lenses. Applies the equity test (20% dilution must raise expected outcome by more than 1.25x). Checks default alive and how close they are to ramen profitable. Time check: building is cheaper (P1/P3 amplified, raise less) but AI compute cost per use (P5 weakened) means checking gross margin. Clear recommendation.

evals.name: model-training-capital
evals.prompt: We're training a specialised foundation model for protein design. Realistically we need around $40M of compute over the next 18 months to get to a model that's competitive. Investors keep telling us to raise an $8M seed first and prove things out. Paul Graham always says raise as little as you need — so should we push back and go for less, or what?
evals.expected_output: Recognises that PG's raise-little logic rested on money not buying speed (P2), which is reversed for model-training companies. Says so explicitly with essay and year. Still applies what holds: start with a cheaper subset and expand (guidetoinvestors 2007), investor herd dynamics. Does not simply repeat 'raise as little as possible'.
